question: How does Java's Comparator demonstrate the Strategy pattern?
title: Comparator as Strategy Pattern in Java
direct_answer: **Comparator** is a ready-made **Strategy**: it encapsulates one pluggable algorithm — how to compare two objects. The sort methods (`Collections.sort`, `List.sort`, `Stream.sorted`) are the **context**; the sorting algorithm (Timsort) is fixed, but the comparison logic is injected. Pass a different `Comparator` and you sort by a different field, with zero change to the sort method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can spot the Strategy pattern living inside the standard library, not just in a textbook diagram
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing Collections.sort knows how to compare your custom objects — it does not; it only knows the sort algorithm and delegates every comparison to the Comparator
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point out that a lambda passed to sort() is an anonymous strategy, and that thenComparing composes strategies just like the GoF intended

sections.title: Comparator as Built-In Strategy Pattern
sections.content:
Java's **Comparator** is the most-used example of the **Strategy pattern** hiding in plain sight. A `Comparator<T>` has a single method, `compare(a, b)`, that returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number to say which object comes first. That single pluggable method *is* the strategy.

The **context** is any sort method — `Collections.sort`, `List.sort`, `Arrays.sort`, or `Stream.sorted`. The sorting algorithm itself (Java uses Timsort) never changes. What changes is the **comparison rule** you hand in. Sort users by name, then by age, then by signup date — same sort method, three different `Comparator` strategies.

It's like a sorting machine on a conveyor belt: the machine's mechanism is fixed, but you swap the *rule card* that tells it which item goes first. Since Java 8, a **lambda** is the shortest way to write that rule card — `(a, b) -> a.price() - b.price()` is an anonymous strategy created inline.

sections.title: Without Comparator-as-strategy — sort logic hardcoded
With Comparator — algorithm fixed, comparison rule injected
Comparator = Strategy, Mapped to the Pattern's Roles
sections.content:
amber|Strategy interface|~The pluggable contract|Comparator<T>|one method: compare(a, b)|returns negative / 0 / positive
blue|Concrete strategies|~The interchangeable rules|byPrice, byName, byStock|lambdas count too|swap freely at runtime
emerald|Context|~Uses a strategy, owns the algorithm|Collections.sort / List.sort|Timsort stays fixed|delegates each comparison
violet|Composition|~Build bigger strategies|thenComparing chains rules|reversed() flips order|nullsFirst handles nulls

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking `sort` knows how to compare your objects.** It does not. It only knows Timsort. Every time it must decide A vs B, it calls *your* `Comparator`. The comparison logic is 100% yours.
- **Not seeing a lambda as a strategy.** `list.sort((a, b) -> ...)` is an anonymous `Comparator` — a full strategy object, just written inline. It is not magic syntax.
- **Confusing `Comparable` with `Comparator`.** `Comparable` is the object's *single natural ordering* (`compareTo`, baked into the class). `Comparator` is an *external, swappable* strategy — that is exactly why it fits the pattern.
- **Hand-writing reversed logic.** Use `comparator.reversed()` and `thenComparing()` to compose strategies instead of duplicating comparison code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Comparator is the strategy** — one method, `compare(a, b)`, returning negative/zero/positive.
- **The sort methods are the context** — Timsort is fixed; the comparison rule is injected.
- **One list, many orderings** — pass a different `Comparator` to sort by a different field, no sort-code change.
- **Lambdas are anonymous strategies** — `(a, b) -> ...` and `Comparator.comparing(...)` create strategies inline.
- **Compose, don't duplicate** — `thenComparing`, `reversed`, and `nullsFirst` build new strategies from existing ones.
- **Comparable vs Comparator** — natural ordering baked into the class vs an external swappable strategy.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Comparator is Java's built-in example of the Strategy pattern. It captures one pluggable algorithm — how to compare two objects — behind a single method called compare. You give it two objects, and it returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number to say which one comes first. That single method is the strategy. The sort methods, like Collections dot sort and List dot sort, are the context. The actual sorting algorithm, which is Timsort in Java, never changes. What changes is the comparison rule you hand in. So I can sort a list of products by price, then sort the same list by stock, then by name, all using the same sort method but passing a different Comparator each time. Each Comparator is a different strategy, swapped at runtime. The sort method doesn't know how to compare my custom objects — it only knows the algorithm. Every time it needs to decide whether A comes before B, it calls the Comparator I passed in. Since Java 8, a lambda is the shortest way to write one of these strategies. When I write list dot sort with a lambda comparing two prices, that lambda is an anonymous Comparator — a real strategy object written inline. And I can compose strategies: comparing by name, then by price when names tie, using thenComparing. The mistake freshers make is thinking sort already knows how to order their objects, or not realizing a lambda is a strategy. Once you see Comparator this way, you realize almost every functional interface in Java — Runnable, Predicate, Function — is the Strategy pattern in disguise.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Comparator is the Strategy pattern that has been in Java since day one — most developers use it daily without ever noticing the pattern underneath.

beats.content: Collections dot sort is the context — the sorting algorithm is fixed. Comparator is the strategy interface — you inject the comparison rule. Sort by name, sort by salary, sort by date: three strategies, one sort method that never changes.

With Java 8 lambdas the strategy collapses to one line: a lambda taking two employees and comparing their salaries. A lambda is just an anonymous strategy. And Comparator dot comparing by name, then comparing by age, composes two strategies in sequence.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: Almost every functional interface in Java is a strategy — Runnable, Predicate, Function, Callable. The Strategy pattern is the foundation of the functional style Java adopted in version 8.

question: What is the Strategy pattern and what problem does it solve?
title: Strategy Pattern Explained
direct_answer: The **Strategy pattern** is a behavioral pattern that puts each algorithm in its own class behind a common **interface**, so the **context** can swap algorithms at runtime via **composition** instead of `if-else`. It solves the growing conditional problem: adding a new behavior means writing a new class, not editing existing code — making the design **open for extension, closed for modification**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the exact smell Strategy removes — the if-else/switch chain that grows with every new variant — and show the polymorphic replacement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing Strategy as 'just use an interface' without showing the before (conditional chain) and after (one class per algorithm) transformation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Stress that selection must move OUT of the context (to a factory or DI); if the context still has the if-else, you only relocated the problem

sections.title: Strategy Pattern Fundamentals
sections.content:
The **Strategy pattern** is a behavioral design pattern that wraps each algorithm in its own class, all implementing a shared **strategy interface**. The **context** holds a reference to that interface and delegates the work — it never knows which concrete algorithm it's running.

Think of checkout: whether you pay by card, UPI, or cash, the cashier follows one step — *accept payment*. The cashier (context) doesn't care how each method works internally; each just fulfills the same contract.

The problem it solves is **conditional complexity**. When one operation has many variants, freshers reach for a giant `if-else`/`switch` on a type field. Every new variant edits that block, risking bugs in the paths you didn't touch. Strategy replaces that branching with **polymorphism**: one interface, many classes, runtime selection. The payoff is the **Open/Closed Principle** — add a new algorithm by adding a class, never by editing the context.

sections.title: Without Strategy — the if-else chain that grows forever
With Strategy — one class per algorithm, context stays closed
Strategy Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Strategy interface|~The shared contract|usually one method|e.g. apply(price)|enables substitution
blue|Concrete strategies|~One class per algorithm|NoDiscount, StudentDiscount|isolated and unit-testable|add new = add class
emerald|Context|~Holds and delegates|has-a strategy|never checks the type|stays closed for change
violet|Selection|~Happens outside|factory or Spring DI|chosen at runtime|keep it out of the context

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Putting the if-else back inside the context.** A `DiscountCalculator` whose method still does `if (type == ...)` just centralizes the mess. The context must never know concrete strategy types.
- **One strategy class with many methods** (`applyStudent()`, `applyBlackFriday()`). That's the conditional in disguise and breaks Single Responsibility — each algorithm should be its own class.
- **Using Strategy when there's only one algorithm** that never changes. The extra abstraction earns nothing; reach for it only when you truly have interchangeable behaviors.
- **Forgetting selection has to live somewhere** — usually a factory, a map, or DI. Strategy moves the choice out of the context, it doesn't delete it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Strategy = family of interchangeable algorithms** behind one interface, chosen at runtime.
- **Replaces if-else/switch** on a type field with polymorphic dispatch.
- **Context is dumb** — it has-a strategy and delegates; it never knows the concrete type.
- **Open/Closed** — new behavior = new class, zero edits to the context.
- **Selection moves out** — to a factory, a map, or Spring DI; never back into the context.
- **Composition over inheritance** — behavior is injected, not inherited.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, puts each one in its own class, and makes them interchangeable behind a common interface. It solves the if-else explosion. Picture a cart checkout. Without Strategy, you write a giant conditional: if the discount type is student do this, else if it's black friday do that, else if it's festive do something else. Every time you add a new discount, you edit that same block and risk breaking the existing branches. With Strategy, you define a DiscountStrategy interface with one method, apply. Then NoDiscount, StudentDiscount, and BlackFriday each implement it. Your Cart class — the context — takes a DiscountStrategy in its constructor and just calls apply. It doesn't know or care which concrete type it got; the JVM dispatches to the right one. Now adding a festive discount means writing one new class. You never touch Cart, and you never retest the other discounts. That's the Open Closed Principle in action — open for extension, closed for modification. The most important thing to say in an interview is where selection happens. The if-else doesn't disappear into the context; it moves out, to a factory or to Spring's dependency injection. If your context still has an if-else picking the strategy, you only relocated the problem. The whole point is that the context stays dumb — it executes whatever strategy it's handed. And under the hood, Strategy is composition over inheritance: the behavior is injected as an object, not locked into a class hierarchy.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Strategy pattern is the cure for a very specific smell — the if-else chain that grows one branch longer every time someone adds a new behavior type.

beats.content: Imagine a checkout service: if the payment type is credit card do this, else if UPI do that, else if cash on delivery do the other thing. Every new payment method means editing this method. That's an Open Closed violation — the class changes for every extension.

Strategy fixes it. Define a PaymentStrategy interface with a single process method. Credit card, UPI, and cash on delivery each implement it with their own logic. PaymentService just holds a PaymentStrategy and calls it — no if-else, no knowledge of which type it got.

content: The context delegates to the strategy — it doesn't choose the algorithm
The strategy is injected from outside — by the caller, a factory, or Spring DI
Adding a new payment method is a new strategy class, with zero changes to the context

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: Java's Comparator is the canonical Strategy example. Collections dot sort is the context; the comparison rule is the strategy you inject. Lambdas make Strategy a one-liner.

question: How do you implement Strategy pattern for a payment system in Java?
title: Strategy Pattern: Payment System Implementation
direct_answer: Define a `PaymentStrategy` interface with a `process()` method, write one concrete class per method (`CreditCardPayment`, `UPIPayment`, `CODPayment`), and inject the chosen strategy into `PaymentService` via the **constructor**. The service calls `process()` blindly — it never checks the payment type. **Selection happens upstream** in a factory, a map, or Spring DI, never inside the service.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you keep the context free of type checks and move selection outside it — the real test of understanding Strategy, not just drawing the interface
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting a switch on paymentType inside PaymentService.process(), which keeps the conditional you were trying to remove
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show Spring auto-wiring a Map<String, PaymentStrategy> so adding a gateway is one new @Component with no edits anywhere else

sections.title: Building a Payment Strategy System
sections.content:
A payment system is the classic Strategy interview question because every method — card, UPI, cash on delivery — has different logic but the same shape: *take an amount, process it, report success*.

The core rule: **`PaymentService` must never contain `if-else` on payment type.** It receives a `PaymentStrategy` and delegates. Each method becomes its own class implementing the interface, so adding crypto next month is one new class, not an edit to the service.

**Where does the choice happen?** Upstream — the controller reads the payment type from the request and asks a **factory** or a **map** for the matching strategy, then hands it to the service. The context stays *dumb*: it knows a `PaymentStrategy` will do the work, nothing more. That dumbness is exactly what makes the system extensible.

sections.title: Without Strategy — service owns a growing switch
With Strategy + Spring — context is dumb, map auto-grows
Payment Strategy — Who Does What
sections.content:
amber|PaymentStrategy|~The contract|one method: process|amount + details in|boolean out
blue|Concrete strategies|~Per gateway|CreditCardPayment, UPIPayment|each validates its own way|add gateway = add class
emerald|PaymentService (context)|~Delegates only|holds a strategy or map|no type checks inside|stays closed for change
violet|Selection|~Upstream choice|controller + factory/map|or Spring DI by bean name|never inside the service

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **A switch inside `process()`.** The whole point is that the context doesn't know payment types. Selection must happen before the strategy reaches the service.
- **Strategies doing unrelated work** — order validation, inventory checks, shipping. Keep a payment strategy to payment concerns only; everything else belongs in other services.
- **`new CreditCardPayment()` inside the service.** That hardcodes one strategy and kills testability. Inject via constructor (or let Spring inject the map).
- **Forgetting the unknown-type case.** A map lookup can return `null` — throw a clear error or supply a default strategy.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **One interface, one class per gateway** — `process(amount, details)` returning success.
- **Context never type-checks** — `PaymentService` delegates, it doesn't decide.
- **Constructor injection** keeps the service immutable and easy to mock in tests.
- **Spring map injection** — `Map<String, PaymentStrategy>` auto-fills by bean name; adding a gateway is one `@Component`.
- **Selection lives upstream** — controller + factory/map/DI choose the strategy.
- **Handle the unknown type** — null check the lookup and fail clearly.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: To implement Strategy for payments, I start with a PaymentStrategy interface that has one method, process, taking the amount and a map of details and returning a boolean. Then I write one concrete class per payment method. CreditCardPayment validates the card number and CVV. UPIPayment checks the VPA format. CashOnDelivery verifies the address. They all implement the same interface, so they're interchangeable. The important part is the context. PaymentService takes a PaymentStrategy — or better, a map of strategies — and just calls process. It never checks the payment type with an if-else; that would defeat the pattern. In Spring this gets really clean. I annotate each strategy with at Component and give it a name. Then PaymentService declares a constructor parameter of type Map of String to PaymentStrategy, and Spring automatically injects every payment strategy bean into that map, keyed by the bean name. At checkout, the service does a map lookup to get the right strategy and calls process. No switch statement anywhere in the service. The selection happens upstream — the controller reads the payment type from the request and passes it down, or a factory resolves it. The mistake freshers make is putting the switch inside process. That just moves the conditional you were trying to remove. The context has to stay dumb. The benefit is huge: adding wallet payments next month means writing one new class annotated with at Component. The map grows automatically and PaymentService doesn't change at all. I'd also mention handling an unknown type — the map lookup can return null, so I throw a clear error or fall back to a default strategy.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: The payment example is where Strategy clicks — but the part interviewers actually grade is whether the service stays free of the switch you started with.

beats.content: Define PaymentStrategy with one method, process, taking a payment request. Write a credit card strategy, a UPI strategy, and a cash on delivery strategy — each handles only its own gateway logic.

PaymentService holds a map from payment method to strategy. At checkout, a lookup replaces the if-else: get the strategy for the chosen method, then call process. No switch, no conditionals inside the service itself.

In Spring, annotate each strategy with at Component. PaymentService gets a map of strategy beans auto-injected, keyed by bean name. Adding a wallet strategy means one new class — the map grows automatically and PaymentService is untouched.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: The selection still has to happen somewhere. It moves to the caller or a factory — not into the context. If PaymentService still has an if-else choosing the strategy, you only moved the problem, you didn't solve it.

question: How do you use Spring's @Qualifier annotation for Strategy pattern-style selection?
title: Strategy Pattern with Spring @Qualifier
direct_answer: When several beans implement one strategy interface, Spring can't autowire it alone — it throws **NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException**. Give each implementation a name and select it with **@Qualifier** for a fixed choice, or inject a **Map<String, Strategy>** that Spring auto-fills with every bean (keyed by bean name) for **runtime** selection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can wire Strategy through Spring's container instead of calling new, and know both the fixed (@Qualifier) and dynamic (Map) approaches
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling new StrategyImpl() inside the context, which bypasses DI and breaks testability and bean lifecycle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Map injection keys by bean name (default = class name, first letter lowercased), and how to combine @Profile for environment-based wiring

sections.title: Spring-Powered Strategy Selection
sections.content:
Strategy naturally produces **many beans of one type** — three classes implementing `ShippingStrategy`, all annotated `@Component`. If a service just autowires `ShippingStrategy`, Spring can't decide which one and throws **NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException**.

Two fixes. For a **fixed** choice known at startup, use **@Qualifier("name")** on the injection point to name the exact bean. For a **runtime** choice from a known set, inject a **`Map<String, ShippingStrategy>`** — Spring populates it with every matching bean, keyed by bean name, and you look up the strategy by a string at request time.

Either way you've combined Strategy with dependency injection: no `new`, fully mockable in tests, and adding a strategy is just adding a `@Component`.

sections.title: Without DI — context hardcodes the strategy
With @Qualifier (fixed) and Map (dynamic)
Spring Strategy Wiring at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|The problem|~Many beans, one type|3 ShippingStrategy beans|plain autowire fails|NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
blue|@Qualifier|~Fixed selection|name on the injection point|wired once at startup|explicit and simple
emerald|Map injection|~Dynamic selection|Map<String, Strategy>|Spring fills by bean name|pick at runtime by key
violet|Why DI not new|~Container benefits|mockable in tests|managed lifecycle|add bean = add @Component

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`new StrategyImpl()` in the context.** Bypasses Spring entirely — no mocking, no lifecycle, no swapping. Always inject.
- **Qualifier on the class but not the injection point.** You must add `@Qualifier` where the bean is *consumed*, not only where it's defined, or Spring still can't disambiguate.
- **Assuming map keys.** The key is the *bean name*. With bare `@Component` it's the class name with the first letter lowercased (`expressShipping`), not `"express"`. A null lookup usually means a wrong key.
- **Forgetting `@Primary` exists.** When one implementation should be the default, mark it `@Primary` instead of qualifying every injection point.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Multiple beans of one type** make a bare autowire throw `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`.
- **@Qualifier("name")** picks a specific bean for a fixed, startup-time choice.
- **Map<String, Strategy>** is auto-filled by Spring for runtime selection by key.
- **Map keys = bean names** — default is the class name, first letter lowercased.
- **Never `new`** a strategy in the context — inject it for testability and lifecycle.
- **@Primary** sets a default when one implementation should usually win.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: When you use Strategy in Spring, you end up with several beans of the same type — say three classes implementing ShippingStrategy, all annotated at Component. If a service just autowires ShippingStrategy, Spring doesn't know which one to give it and throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. There are two clean fixes. The first is at Qualifier, for a fixed choice. You give each bean a name, then on the injection point — the constructor parameter — you add at Qualifier with the name you want, like express. Spring finds that exact bean and wires it once at startup. The second, and more powerful, approach is map injection for runtime selection. You declare a constructor parameter of type Map of String to ShippingStrategy. Spring automatically fills that map with every ShippingStrategy bean, using the bean name as the key. Now at runtime you do a map lookup with a string — like the shipping type the user chose — and call the strategy you get back. The key thing to know is that the map keys are bean names. If you write at Component with an explicit name like express, the key is express. If you just write at Component with no name, the key defaults to the class name with the first letter lowercased. A null lookup almost always means the key doesn't match the actual bean name. The big mistake is calling new ExpressShipping inside the service. That throws away everything the container gives you — you can't mock it in tests, you lose lifecycle management, and you can't swap implementations without editing code. Always inject. And if one implementation should be the default, mark it at Primary instead of qualifying every single injection point.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Spring turns Strategy into almost no code — the framework can wire every implementation into a map for you, keyed by bean name.

beats.content: The at Qualifier annotation handles a fixed choice: name each bean, then on the injection point add at Qualifier with that name to pull the exact implementation you always want. Explicit and simple.

Map injection is better for a dynamic choice. Annotate all strategies with at Component, then inject a map of String to strategy into the service. Spring fills it with every bean, keyed by bean name, so at runtime you just look up the one you need. Adding a strategy class registers it in the map automatically.

speakable_v2.cap: gotcha: Map keys follow Spring's default bean naming — usually the class name with the first letter lowercased. If a lookup returns null, check the key matches the real bean name, not what you assumed.

question: How is Strategy pattern different from simple polymorphism via inheritance?
title: Strategy Pattern vs Inheritance Polymorphism
direct_answer: Inheritance binds behavior at **compile time** through an IS-A hierarchy — once you create a `CreditCardProcessor`, it's fixed. Strategy uses **composition (HAS-A)** to inject behavior, so the same context can swap algorithms at **runtime** and compose them freely. Both use polymorphism; the difference is *when* and *how* behavior is bound — which is why the GoF say **favor composition over inheritance**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you grasp the IS-A vs HAS-A trade-off and can name a case where inheritance can't change behavior post-construction but Strategy can
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling them identical because both use polymorphism, missing that inheritance locks behavior at instantiation while Strategy swaps it at runtime
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the combinatorial-explosion argument: N behaviors x M variants needs N*M subclasses, but composing strategies stays linear

sections.title: Inheritance vs Composition in Behavior Modeling
sections.content:
Both Strategy and inheritance use polymorphism, so freshers call them the same. The real difference is **IS-A vs HAS-A**.

With **inheritance**, behavior is baked into the class hierarchy. `CreditCardProcessor extends PaymentProcessor` overrides `process()` — but the moment you write `new CreditCardProcessor()`, that object is *forever* a card processor. You can't make it process UPI later.

With **Strategy**, the context *has-a* strategy injected from outside. The same `PaymentService` can take a card strategy today and a UPI strategy tomorrow — or swap mid-run via a setter. Inheritance also can't easily *combine* behaviors: card + fraud-check + loyalty would explode into many subclasses, while strategies compose. That's why the Gang of Four say **favor composition over inheritance** — and Strategy is that principle made concrete.

sections.title: Strategy vs Inheritance
sections.content:
| Aspect | Inheritance (IS-A) | Strategy (HAS-A) |
|---|---|---|
| Behavior binding | Compile-time, in the hierarchy | Runtime, via injection/setter |
| Flexibility | Fixed once instantiated | Swappable any time |
| Combining behaviors | Needs many subclasses (N×M) | Compose/chain strategies (linear) |
| Code reuse | Shared base-class methods | Shared via the strategy contract |
| Testing | Instantiate a concrete subclass | Inject a mock strategy |
| Best when | Subclasses share real implementation | Behavior varies, structure stays same |

sections.title: Which One to Reach For
sections.content:
amber|Inheritance (IS-A)|~Behavior is identity|Dog barks because it IS a Dog|locked at construction|use for shared real code
blue|Strategy (HAS-A)|~Behavior is injected|car picks toll rule by day|swap at runtime|use when behavior varies
emerald|Binding time|~The deciding question|will it change after new?|yes -> Strategy|no, intrinsic -> inheritance
violet|Combining|~Many behaviors at once|subclasses explode (N x M)|strategies compose linearly|favor composition (GoF)

sections.title: Inheritance — behavior locked at construction
Strategy — behavior injected and composable
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **"They're the same — both use polymorphism."** The mechanism is shared, but inheritance is IS-A (locked at construction) and Strategy is HAS-A (swappable at runtime). That structural gap is the whole answer.
- **Missing the binding time.** `new CreditCardProcessor()` fixes behavior forever; `service.setStrategy(new Upi())` changes it on the fly.
- **Subclassing for tiny variance** — `PaymentForUSA`, `PaymentForEU` when only a region rule differs. One context + region strategies is cleaner.
- **Forgetting inheritance still wins sometimes** — when subclasses genuinely share a lot of implementation (a `Vehicle` base with real `start()`/`stop()` code).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **IS-A vs HAS-A** — inheritance puts behavior in the hierarchy; Strategy injects it as an object.
- **Binding time** — inheritance locks behavior at construction; Strategy swaps it at runtime.
- **Combining behaviors** — subclasses explode combinatorially; strategies compose linearly.
- **Testing** — mock a strategy easily vs subclassing for tests.
- **GoF rule** — favor composition over inheritance; Strategy embodies it.
- **Inheritance still fits** when subclasses share substantial real implementation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Both Strategy and inheritance rely on polymorphism, so people assume they're the same. The real difference is when and how behavior gets bound. With inheritance, you define behavior by overriding methods in subclasses. The moment you instantiate a class — say, new CreditCardProcessor — that object's behavior is locked in. It will always do card logic; you can't turn it into a UPI processor later. The behavior is tied to the class type at compile time. That's an IS-A relationship. Strategy uses composition instead — a HAS-A relationship. The context, like PaymentService, holds a reference to a strategy object that's injected from outside through a constructor or setter. So at runtime you can give it a card strategy today and a UPI strategy tomorrow, or even swap it mid-execution, without changing the context. The other big difference is combining behaviors. Suppose you need card payment plus fraud checking plus loyalty points. With inheritance you'd end up with subclasses for every combination — that's a combinatorial explosion. With Strategy you write a fraud-checking strategy that wraps any payment strategy, and you compose them. The subclass count stays linear instead of exploding. The Gang of Four summarized this as favor composition over inheritance, and Strategy is the poster child. Now, inheritance isn't always wrong. When subclasses genuinely share a lot of real implementation — like a Vehicle base class with concrete start and stop methods that Car and Bike reuse — inheritance is the right tool. But when behavior varies independently and the structure stays the same, Strategy wins because of runtime flexibility and easy testing — you just inject a mock strategy.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Strategy and inheritance both use polymorphism, yet one freezes behavior the instant you call new, and the other lets you swap it whenever you like.

beats.content: With inheritance polymorphism, the algorithm is tied to the class. A Car subclass overrides calculate toll and that's fixed. If toll rules change on weekends, you'd subclass Car again or add conditional logic inside the method.

With Strategy, the same Car class holds a toll-strategy reference. You can swap in a weekend toll strategy at runtime without touching Car. The algorithm changes independently of the object. That's composition over inheritance — the Gang of Four's own recommendation.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: Use inheritance when behavior is intrinsic to type identity — a Dog barks because it IS a Dog. Use Strategy when behavior varies independently of type — a car uses different toll rules by day and time, not by what kind of car it is.
